text:
Dana, I have the wrap-up on the Harbor Street intake pilot for the quarter. We ran the new triage form at the front desk from March 3 through May 30, a little later than planned because the printer in room 2 kept jamming on consent sheets. Ruth from nursing did most of the training, and Bashir covered evening shifts when two front desk staff were out sick.

The number to look at is wait time. Patients who went through the new form waited an average of 14 minutes before seeing a nurse, down from 31 minutes in the same weeks last year. The peaks were Monday and Thursday mornings, and that is where most complaints came from. Two people said the tablet froze when the clinic wifi dropped, which happened on eleven days. Each one is logged in the pilot tracker so we can show IT exactly when it failed.

Overall I think the pilot worked. Staff rated it 4.2 out of 5 on the short survey, and the no-show rate barely moved. Dr. Okafor advised that we keep the form at Harbor Street and hold off on Eastgate until IT fixes the wifi, and Ruth agreed when we talked Friday. Pedro wants a call before anything goes to the board, so I have put thirty minutes on his calendar for Tuesday.

I attached the tracker and the raw survey export. Tell me if you want the numbers split by provider.

Marcus, the Cold Dock reslotting project is further along than last week, but one piece is stuck. The pick-path model is finished and Yusuf has it running against last month's order history. Right now the model says we can cut walking distance for the picking crew by about 18 percent if we move the fast-moving SKUs closer to pack station three. That number is a simulation, not a measured result, and I do not trust it until we run a real two-day test on the east aisles.

The stuck piece is the cold zone. Freezer racks are bolted to the floor, so every move there needs a forklift and a second person, and Ines is the only one on second shift certified on the lift. She has to sign off on each pallet move, which means the schedule is really her schedule. I am asking the planning group to hold Tuesday and Wednesday nights for her so the test does not slide into October.

Two colleagues have questions I cannot answer yet. Priya wants to know whether the new slot labels will survive condensation in the cold room, and the label vendor has not replied to Monday's email. Gabe thinks cycle counts will look worse for a few weeks after the move, which is probably true, so I have told him we should warn the client in writing before we start.

Next steps are simple. Yusuf finishes the aisle map by Thursday, I send the test plan to the site leads on Friday, and we pick a start date on the Monday call. Tell me if anything here conflicts with the Q4 shipping plan.

Tomasz, the Reading Ladder pilot ended last Friday, and here is what we saw across the sixth grade classes at Riverbend. Kim ran the morning groups in rooms 104 and 106, and Oluwaseun took the afternoon sessions in the library. We started in January with 62 students reading below grade level, and by spring 49 of them had moved up at least one band on the district benchmark.

The biggest surprise was attendance. Our first month had almost no decline in participation, which I did not expect given how many kids hold after-school jobs. The reason, I think, is that Kim started calling home every Wednesday, and several families told us they were unaware the program existed until she called. We should keep that routine even though it costs her a few hours each week.

Not everything worked. The audio books in the Ladder kit kept skipping on the older library laptops, and Oluwaseun spent two weeks swapping hardware before we gave up and bought tablets. We also never got the reading logs into the student portal, so teachers copied the numbers by hand. Tomasz, I would like to ask the district for money to finish the portal, and I drafted a short request for you to review before Monday.

Ferris, a quick update on the Quill assay before Thursday's group meeting. Last week Nadia ran the first full plate with the new primer set, and the bands came up clean on 14 of the 16 isolates. The two that failed were both from the Tuesday batch, which Sanjay thinks was stored a day too long at room temperature. He is pulling a fresh aliquot now.

The magenta dye on the gel was faint, which made the band sizing hard to read by eye. Nadia switched to the imager on the second run, and the sizes match the ladder within the expected range. We still need to confirm the sequence for the four isolates that came back with odd bands, and Omar has booked the sequencing core for Monday. Until those results are in, I would not put any of the numbers in the grant draft.

Next week we are going to repeat the whole run with the old primer set side by side, so we have a clean comparison. The plan is to finish by the 20th if the core turns the traces around quickly. I will bring the gel images and the lane map to the meeting, and I expect Nadia to present the sizing table. Let me know if you want the protocol changes written up before then.

Lena and Hakim, the spring menu launch at Tamarind Bakery is going to need more planning than the winter one did. On April 6 we will put the lemon cardamom loaf and the rhubarb galette on the case for the first time. Lena is going to set the recipe weights by the 28th, and Hakim will order the rhubarb from the Kessler farm before the price jumps. We will run a two-week test on the small batch oven before we commit to any quantities, because the galette crust will tear if the dough sits too long in the walk-in.

The patio is the real question. If the forecast looks windy, the umbrellas will not hold and we will be moving chairs in and out all morning. I want a plan for that, maybe a shaker of flour and powdered sugar kept by the register for the table cloths, and a rule that anything outside goes back indoors by noon if the gusts pass twenty miles an hour. Hakim, can you check whether the lease covers outdoor seating, since our obligations there were written before we added the patio.

I will cost out both menus over the weekend and send the margins Monday. My plan is to keep the cinnamon twist and the sourdough on the rotation, because the regulars will notice if those disappear. We will also review the sales from the first four weeks on May 3 and decide whether the galette stays. Lena, please bring the old prep sheets so we can compare labor hours.

Team, the Sunday desk is halfway through the shift overhaul, and I want to lay out where things stand before the schedule posts Friday. Ana now runs the 6 a.m. to 2 p.m. slot with Malik on copy, and Jun covers the late web push. The new layout keeps one producer on the Ledger homepage at all times, which is the piece the old system never managed.

The troubling part is the overnight gap. We still have no one reliably watching the wire between 1 and 4 a.m., and two breaking stories last month sat for almost forty minutes before anyone noticed. Malik suggested a split where the night editor takes the wire and the web producer handles only alerts. I think that is the right direction, even though it adds a shift we have not budgeted for yet.

Our dominant traffic still comes from morning email and the app push, so the early hours matter more than they used to. I am asking each of you to send me your availability for the next six weeks by Wednesday, and I will build the rota from there. Please flag any conflicts with court dates or school pickups now rather than later.

Imani, the Mill Creek branch reopened on September 12, and I want to write up what happened during the closure while it is still fresh. The contractor, Haddad Builders, pulled the old carpet in June and found water damage behind the north wall, which pushed the schedule back nearly six weeks. Facilities approved the extra money, and Rosa handled the public notices so patrons knew where to pick up holds.

The biggest problem was the predecessor's shelving plan. The old layout had been drawn for 1998 circulation, and when Tobias ran the counts we found the children's section was crammed into a corner nobody could reach in a wheelchair. We reworked the aisles in July on the same budget, which meant cutting two study carrels. Several regulars were unaware of the change until they walked in, and the front desk took a lot of questions that first week.

Circulation is back to about 92 percent of last year, and the holds shelf is busier than before. I think the reopening went well, but we should document the water issue properly before anyone forgets it. Tobias has the moisture readings, and I would like the file sent to the district office by the end of the month. Thanks for approving the overtime for the move, because it saved us a weekend.

Gordon, next month Line 4 will switch from the old cap sealer to the new Vantor model, and this email covers how we plan to do it. The changeover will take three shifts, starting Monday March 9. Gabriela will take the first shift and set the torque values from the vendor sheet, and Desmond will run the validation parts on second shift to check the seal rate.

We will know quickly whether this works. The target is a seal pass rate above 99.2 percent on the first 500 caps, and anything below that counts as a categorical failure that stops the line until a supervisor signs off. I am proposing that we hold a spare cap head in the cage, because the last time we had a jam, the replacement took eleven days to ship from the vendor's plant in Ohio.

Please send me your feedback on the maintenance schedule by Thursday. I will be out Monday and Tuesday, so Gabriela is going to lead the morning huddle and make the final call on the torque settings. Once the trial run is done, we will write up the numbers and decide whether Line 5 gets the same upgrade in the summer.

Rafi, the walk-in is a mess again, and I need us to fix the labeling system for good. Right now every station uses its own tape color, so the sauce team's lids look the same as the pastry team's, and Dani keeps tossing containers she thinks are expired. We are switching to a color code: magenta for anything made in the last 24 hours, yellow for two days, and plain white for dry goods.

The peaks are the problem. From 5 to 8 p.m. the line is running three reorders at once, and labels get written in a rush or not at all. I see the same thing on the Saturday lunch shift. Lupe says the printer by the pass takes too long to warm up, so she writes by hand, which is fine as long as the date is legible. Two of the colleagues asked me to add a time column too, and I think that is a good call.

I am also giving Hollis the weekly audit. He walks the walk-in every Monday at 2 p.m., logs what he finds, and sends me the sheet before service. That gives us a number to track, so the goal is fewer than three violations a week. I put the new labels in the back cabinet and the code sheet on the clipboard by the door. Please read it before Wednesday's prep.

Everyone, the Eastside Pantry fall volunteer schedule is out of balance, and I want your input before we lock it in. Last month we ran the Saturday sort with only four people and had to pull Bea off the front desk to help with the cooler. Trevor covered three weekday shifts that were supposed to belong to other people, which is not a sustainable arrangement.

Here is what the sign-up sheet shows so far. We have about 60 percent of the Tuesday shifts filled, but Thursday evenings are nearly empty, and the donated pallets from the regional warehouse arrive around 5:30 p.m. Ana advised us to move two of the Thursday runs to Friday morning, which would mean the drivers lose their evenings, so I am not sure yet. Our insurance obligations also say every shift needs at least one trained lead, and right now only six people hold that certificate.

My plan is to hold a short training session on October 14 so we have ten certified leads by the end of the month. In the meantime, could everyone who is free on Thursday evenings reply to this thread by Friday? I will update the schedule over the weekend and post the final version Monday. Thank you all, honestly, because the pantry does not run without you.

Kit, I owe you a proper update after the weekend, so here it is. We drove down to Galveston on Saturday morning with the blue cooler packed to the lid and the radio turned all the way up. Uncle Lorne had already claimed the picnic table by the water before the rest of us got out of the van. Dorrie brought her beloved cast iron skillet, which she swears has never once been washed with soap, and she fried the first batch of hushpuppies right there on the gravel while the kids chased seagulls.

The oysters were the real event, though. Pawpaw shucked about four dozen with that dented knife he has kept since the Carter administration, and he waved it at anyone who tried to help him. Little Pim got a small cut on her thumb. It was nothing serious, but she cried long enough that we had to dig the bandages out of the glovebox. Mom sprinkled too much pepper on everything, as usual, and Lorne spent the rest of lunch drinking water and insisting he was fine.

We stayed until the sun dropped low and the mosquitoes showed up in a crowd. On the drive home Pim fell asleep with the cooler lid in her lap, and Dorrie kept humming the same three notes from some old radio song. Next time you have to come, and bring the good hot sauce, not the grocery store kind that tastes like vinegar. I'll send the photos tonight once the upload finishes. Love you, and tell Ruby the lemon bars were a hit. Sunny

Ines, thank you so much for letting me borrow the green Volvo this week. I know how much you love that automobile, and I keep reminding myself to be extra careful with the clutch. It is the first thing I notice when I sit down, the way the seat still smells faintly of your dog Biscuit and that peppermint gum you always keep in the cup holder. Honestly it feels like a little piece of your life rides along with me every time I turn the key.

The garage door is still the main problem in our house. Wendell says there is a crack along the bottom panel that lets all the cold air in, and he thinks the spring is ready to give out any day. He has a plan to patch it on Sunday, although he has been saying that for three Sundays in a row. Meanwhile the kids have decided the driveway is a skating rink whenever it rains, so I am the one who keeps the bag of salt near the back steps.

The lasagna dish you dropped off is still on our counter, scrubbed and waiting. I am going to fill it with something tonight, probably the chicken and rice thing Mom always makes when somebody is sick, and I'll bring it over before the weekend. Tell Biscuit I said hello and that he owes me a walk. We really do appreciate you more than I know how to put in a text. Call me when you are free and we will sort out the garage door together. Warmly, Teodor

Vesna, I finally got the dates locked in for the trip, so here is the plan. We will fly into Asheville on the Thursday before the wedding and drive the rest of the way out on Friday morning. Nell asked everyone to be there by noon for the photos, which gives us time to unpack and maybe find a coffee shop that doesn't close at three in the afternoon. I already have the directions saved on my phone, though I'm sure we will lose signal somewhere in the hills.

Wherever we end up staying, I want a place with a porch. Hollis is going to bring his guitar, and he will try to play every song he knows while we eat. I also need a proper outfit for the ceremony. My green dress is still hanging in the closet, but I think I'll ask Pim to help me find something with pockets, because I always misplace my keys at the worst possible moment. We will need to sort out the rental car too, since the one that was booked does not fit all six of us and the bags.

The mountain drive is going to be beautiful. I'll be checking the map the whole way, and at some point the GPS will probably tell us we're somewhere near longitude 82 degrees west, which is a number I plan to laugh at for the rest of my life. Send me your flight number as soon as you have it. We'll meet at baggage claim and get pancakes from the place by the exit, the one with the tiny plastic cows on the shelf. It is going to be a good week, I just know it. Love, Dana

Marisol, I am sorry it took me so long to write after the move. We finished unloading the truck on the last Sunday in June, and I'm still finding boxes labeled kitchen misc in the hallway. The new place sits right above a small creek that runs down behind the old mill, and on the first night we sat on the back steps listening to the water. Our son Ansel said it sounded like someone whispering, and that kept him awake for a good hour.

The renaming of our street was the funniest part. The city decided last winter to change Mill Road to Ferry Lane, and the sign on our corner was still the old one when we signed the papers. The movers kept insisting we lived on a different road, and the mail carrier had to check the house number twice before handing me a package. I think the whole town is confused about it, which somehow makes me feel better about my own tangled directions.

The house needs some work. The porch rail is loose, the back door sticks in humid weather, and the basement smells like wet cardboard. My brother Ivo came over with a toolbox and spent an entire Saturday tightening screws, and he refused to take any money for it. We ordered pizza, watched the river from the kitchen window, and talked until the sky turned orange. You should visit once the garden is in. I'll make the lemon bars you like, and we can walk down to the waterways together. Hugs to everyone, Nadia

Ruthie, quick note about Pawpaw's party. Everyone is invited to the lake cabin on Saturday the 14th, starting around two. Mom is in charge of invitations and she is being very dramatic about the guest list. Pawpaw says he wants no speeches, just hot dogs and a cooler full of root beer. Dad cooks the burgers on the old grill every year, and he refuses to let anyone else touch the tongs.

Here's the spooky part. Aunt Pim decided the party needs a theme, so now we're all supposed to dress like it's the year Pawpaw was born. Nobody told her that was 1946, so Lorne plans to show up in a bedsheet and claim he is a ghost from the old days. The porch light flickers whenever you walk under it, which makes the whole cabin feel a little haunted after dark. Pim says it's perfect. I say we should all bring flashlights.

Let me know what you're bringing for dessert. My plan is the blueberry crumble, the one with the crunchy top, and maybe a tray of brownies for the kids. Brigid says she can drive the van if Hollis is too tired after his long shift. Also, if you see Wendell before Saturday, tell him the lake will be cold, so he needs to bring a sweater. He always forgets. That's all for now. Love, Bea

Jonah, you deserve a real apology for missing your birthday dinner last month. I had promised I'd be there, and then the week got away from me. Dad's knee surgery moved to a Tuesday, and I spent most of that evening in the hospital parking garage trying to get a signal. I know it is no excuse, but I hope the cake was good and that Marisol saved you a slice.

Now I need a favor, and I know it's a big one. I'm flying to the craft fair in Duluth next week because my ceramics booth got accepted and I'm officially an exhibitor. It's a small thing, but it is the first time anyone has asked me to display my work. I'd love it if you could feed Biscuit the cat and water the fern on the windowsill. The fern is fussy and drops leaves when it's thirsty, so please use the blue watering can, not the big jug.

The whole thing has been incremental, honestly. I have been practicing one bowl at a time, adding a small detail to each and trying not to get frustrated when the glaze runs. Last week I finally got a set of four that looked right, and my roommate Teddy said they were better than anything from the last show. If you can help for those few days, I'll bring you back a mug and dinner when I get home. Let me know by Friday so I can leave the spare key with the landlord. Thanks for putting up with me. Anna

Dear Aunt Lise, you're going to laugh, but June made it to the finals of the county piano competition. She played a Chopin nocturne she had been practicing since March, and her hands were shaking so hard before she started that I thought she would drop her music. The judges sat in a row at a folding table in the church basement, and June bowed to them like a visiting professor. Two of the judges were smiling by the end, which was more than I expected.

We drove home afterward with the windows open and the radio off. Grandma Ilse had already cooked a huge pot of chicken soup, the kind with dill and a little too much pepper, and she set out a tray of buttered rolls. Uncle Teo arrived late with a cake from the bakery on Harbor Street, the lemon one with the thick frosting that June always asks for. We ate on the back steps while the neighbor's dog barked at the sprinklers and nobody wanted to go inside.

The best part was watching June eat two slices of cake and then fall asleep on the couch in her good dress. She is still wearing the small silver pin the judges gave her, and she has already asked when she can enter next year. I told her we would see. Thanks for the card with the twenty dollar bill. She wants to spend it on sheet music, so you will probably hear about that soon. Give my love to Rafe and the girls, and tell them June says hello. Talk soon, Mara

Gil, it has been way too long since I wrote a real letter, so bear with me. I'm living in a tiny apartment above the bakery on Cedar Street, and every morning the smell of bread wakes me up before the alarm does. My roommate Hugo is still building model ships on the kitchen table, which means I eat breakfast surrounded by sawdust and tiny rigging ropes. He is convinced the boats will make him famous someday. I'm mostly convinced he needs a bigger table.

Work is busy but good. I spend most days at the water district office, mapping the old drainage ditches so the city can decide which ones to clean first. It sounds dull, but I like it more than I expected. Yesterday I walked the length of the eastern channel with a guide named Noor, who knows every heron by name. She showed me where the waterways split into three branches and explained how spring floods carry silt down toward the reservoir. I took two hundred photos, and all of them look the same to me.

On weekends I cook big pots of lentil stew and invite whoever is around. Last Saturday six people crowded into the kitchen, and somebody kept adding pepper until everyone's eyes watered. I told them you would have loved it. The dog next door, a scruffy little terrier named Mochi, sits outside the door every afternoon and waits for scraps. He is a menace, but I'm fond of him. Come visit in the fall if you can. We will rent canoes and paddle the whole river until our arms give out. Write back soon. Ines

Hi everyone, here is the plan for the reunion next August. We are meeting at the old campground in Kestrel Ridge on Friday night, and the whole weekend will be part camping, part cabin, and a lot of food. Wren has already volunteered to plan the games for the kids, and Tobiah promised to bring the enormous tent that fits twelve people, though nobody has ever seen him set it up.

Each family is responsible for one meal. We'll take Saturday breakfast, and my mother wants to make her famous cinnamon rolls, which take three hours and a lot of patience. Cousin Dev and his partner will handle Saturday dinner. They plan to grill fish from the lake if the rangers allow it. Sunday brunch belongs to whoever arrives last, which I'm told is my brother, so I'm already preparing a speech of apology.

I also need everyone's ideas for outfits. The theme is "old-school road trip," which means sunglasses, flannel shirts, and maybe a hat or two. I'm thinking about borrowing my dad's old automobile for the parade we're holding on Saturday afternoon. It is a faded green wagon with a cracked seat, but it runs, and it has the loudest horn in the family. Send me your measurements if you want a costume made. Let me know by March so I can order fabric. I can't wait to see all of you there. Love, Pilar

Oren, thanks again for helping with the attic last weekend. I know it wasn't fun hauling boxes down that narrow ladder, and I'm sorry the bats startled you. The house listed on Monday, and the realtor says we'll get a showing every day this week. We have already painted the front room back to the pale yellow Mom picked in 1992, because Carla insists buyers love something familiar.

The renaming part is the strangest. The county decided last year to change our street from Alder Drive to Alder Hollow, so every piece of paper we own has the wrong name on it. The closing lawyer had to draft a special note for the deed, and she laughed about it the whole time. We are keeping the old sign by the mailbox, though, because it's the only thing in the yard that still looks like home.

Now the favor. Could you help us run the yard sale on Saturday morning? Mom wants the rocking chair and the box of old records out front, and she'll bring the coffee. I'm not sure whether the spooky Halloween decorations should go in the sale or the attic, since the kids keep insisting on hanging them for the buyers. The old Buick still needs a new battery, and I'm thinking of parking it on the street so people can see it. If you take the first hour, I'll buy you a sandwich from the deli on Main Street. Thanks, friend. Gwen

So the toilet in our upstairs bathroom kept running all night last March, and I finally got tired of listening to it. My brother Dev said it was probably the flapper, but I wanted to be sure before I went to the hardware store. I pulled the tank lid off and looked at the fill valve first. The float arm was sitting too high and the water kept spilling into the overflow tube, which is why the tank never stopped filling. The flapper itself looked a little warped around the edge, so I bought both parts at the store by the train station.

Before I touched anything I photocopied the little diagram from the back of the old box, because the instructions that came with the new valve were boring and half erased. I shut the water off at the valve behind the toilet, flushed to drain the tank, and sponged out the last cup of water. Unscrewing the old fill valve took a locking nut and a lot of patience. The new one clicked into the same hole, and I trimmed the refill tube so it sat about an inch above the water line.

The flapper was the easy part. I hooked the chain to the lift arm with about an inch of slack, then ran the water back on and let the tank fill. The float came up to the mark on the tube and the water stopped on its own. I flushed three times just to watch the flapper seal, and the bowl stayed quiet. If yours is still running, check the chain length first, then the float height, because those two cause almost every case like this one. Post a photo if you get stuck and I'll look at it.

My sourdough starter has a bit of an attitude this week, so bear with me while I explain what I actually do. Every morning I pour off the grey liquid on top, then feed the jar equal weights of flour and water, usually fifty grams each to fifty of the starter. The jar lives on the counter by the window, and the rubber band marks where it should rise. When it doubles in about four hours, it is ready to build dough with.

For the loaf itself I mix three hundred grams of the bubbly starter with nine hundred grams of water and stir until the mixture looks like milky tea. Then I add the flour, which is a blend of bread flour and a little whole wheat, and let it rest for forty minutes before the salt goes in. Salt is the one part people skip, and the dough goes slack without it. I do a set of stretch and folds every half hour for two hours, which builds the gluten structure without any kneading at all. The dough mostly does the work anyway.

The recipe below serves four people with a generous slice each, so one loaf is plenty for a weeknight. After the bulk rest I shape the dough into a tight round, let it sit for twenty minutes, then flip it into a floured basket and cover it. Overnight in the fridge gives the crumb a sour tang I actually like, and I bake it in a preheated Dutch oven at 500 degrees with the lid on for twenty minutes. Then the lid comes off and the crust goes deep brown. Let it cool at least an hour before cutting, or the inside will be gummy.

Okay Maya, you asked how I plan to handle the household budget once the new lease kicks in, so here is the setup. First I will pull the bank exports for the last three months as CSV files and drop them into one spreadsheet. Each row becomes a transaction, and I will sort them by category with a short column for the merchant. Tagging will be the boring part, but it tells me exactly where the money went.

Next I will set a monthly target for each category rather than a single total. Rent comes out first at the fixed amount, then utilities, then groceries and transport. The leftover money goes into a savings column, and I will move it to the high yield account on the first Friday of every month. Dinners out will get a hard cap, and once that cap is hit the card gets put away for the rest of the month. I expect that rule to be annoying for about two weeks and then not matter at all.

After a month of this, I will compare the actual numbers against the plan and adjust the targets. My guess is groceries will run over, and the streaming subscriptions will turn out to be three services nobody watches. I will send you the spreadsheet link so you can see the summary tab, and you can tell me if I missed anything. Once it runs smoothly, I will set a calendar reminder for the last day of each month to review the exports and update the sheet. That habit is the whole point, so I will keep it simple.

Quick note for anyone wondering how I get my beagle to walk without yanking my arm off. His name is Waffles, he is two, and he thinks every squirrel is a personal invitation. What works for us is a simple stop and go. The moment the leash goes tight I stop walking, and I do not say anything. He looks back, the leash goes slack, and only then do we move again. It is boring to watch but it teaches him that pulling gets him nothing.

I use a front clip harness instead of a collar, because the clip on the chest turns his body back toward me when he lunges. The treats stay in a pouch on my left hip. Every time he walks beside me with a loose lead, he gets a small piece of chicken, and I keep the pieces tiny so he does not get full. Short sessions work best for a beagle, around ten minutes in the living room, then a sniff break. He loses interest fast if the lesson drags on.

When the squirrels show up, I turn us around before he locks up. Reversing direction is the quickest way I have found to break the fixation without a fight. My trainer friend Ellen gave me the idea, and she recommended two trainers in the area for the harder cases. If you are looking for referrals, ask at your vet clinic first, since they usually know who is good with reactive dogs. Consistency matters more than the gear, so pick one method and stick with it for a month before you judge it.

Last winter I turned an old desktop tower into a home media server, and it took most of a weekend. I installed a fresh copy of Ubuntu on a single SSD, then put the four spinning drives into a simple RAID set for the movie library. The tower had only 8 gigs of memory, so I added two sticks for 32 total. Everything runs off the case fans, which were the loudest part of the build. Looking back, I should have replaced those fans first.

For the software I picked Plex, mostly because my cousin Rahul already uses it and kept sending me screenshots. I set up the libraries pointing at folders named by year and title, since Plex is picky about that and the scanner mangled anything messy. The first scan took about six hours over Wi-Fi, so I moved the tower to a wired connection in the den. After that, the library pulled artwork and subtitles for nearly everything. The only files that refused to play were a few old AVI rips, and transcoding fixed them.

The drive setup complies with the basic rule I wanted, which was that one dead disk should not cost me the whole library. I mirrored the important folders to a cheap external drive every Sunday with a script that I wrote in an afternoon. Remote access worked on the first try once I opened the port on the router, though I switched to a private tunnel after that. The server serves the living room TV, my phone on the bus, and my sister's laptop when she visits. My only real mistake was skipping the backup until the second month.

Long story short, my grandmother's walnut dresser had a chipped corner on the top drawer, and I fixed it myself over two evenings. The damage was a bubble of veneer that had lifted off the plywood core, about the size of a playing card. I have done a little woodworking before, mostly boxes and shelves, but veneer repair was new to me. The trick I learned is that you have to lift the loose piece gently with a thin putty knife and never force it.

First I cleaned the old glue out of the gap with a dental pick and a damp cloth. Then I slid a little hide glue under the lifted edge and pressed it flat with a warm iron on low heat, with a scrap of wax paper in between so the iron did not scorch the finish. I weighted it with a stack of books and a cutting board for a full day. Most of the work was waiting, which I did not love, but the seam disappeared once the clamps came off.

For the surface I matched the color with a walnut stain and a thin coat of shellac, then sanded lightly with 320 grit so it blended into the edges. Shellac dries fast, so I built it up in five quick coats instead of one heavy one. The repaired corner still shows if you look closely, but my mom says it looks more like the original now. Lesson learned: keep a scrap of the same veneer around the house, because you will need it for the next chip.

Every time I sit down with a new song, the first thing I play is the tonic chord, because it tells me where home is. In the key of G that is a G major, so I start there and let the rest of the progression orbit around it. Barre chords are the wall most beginners hit, and my own wall was the F chord. I still find the F shape a little rough, but I can play it cleanly now after months of boring repetition on the couch.

The barre finger takes most of the pressure, and it hurts until the calluses come in. I keep my thumb centered behind the neck and roll my index finger slightly onto its side, so the bony edge does the pressing instead of the flat pad. My teacher Dana says to play the chord slowly with only four strings first, then bring in the fifth and sixth once the sound rings clean. She is right, and the strings stop buzzing when I stop rushing.

I practice in a short loop of three chords, the tonic, the subdominant, and the dominant, and I play it with a metronome set around sixty. When the chord changes feel smooth I bump the tempo up by five beats. Strumming is the other half, and I keep my wrist loose so the sound stays even across the strings. Once the barre sounds clear on every string, I move on to real songs. Until then, the metronome stays on and the fancy stuff waits.

Next spring I am building two raised beds along the back fence, and I already have the plan worked out. Each bed will be eight feet long, which serves the fence layout well and leaves room to walk around them. I will use untreated cedar boards, two inches thick, screwed into corner posts. Cedar will cost more than pine, but it will hold up for years without rotting. I will cut all the boards this weekend at the lumber yard so I can stack them in the garage.

The soil mix is where I will spend the real money. I plan to fill the bottom foot with coarse wood chips and leaves, then cover them with a layer of compost and topsoil in roughly equal parts. The beds will drain well and warm up faster in April, which means I can plant the lettuces early. My neighbor Tomas already runs a community plot, and he has agreed to act as the liaison with the HOA, so the fence and the water line should be approved before I break ground.

I will run a soaker hose on a timer, because hand watering in July is a chore I do not want. Tomatoes go on the south end where the sun hits longest, and the basil and herbs go near the gate so they are easy to reach while cooking. Next fall I will top the beds with fresh compost again and let the leaves break down over winter. My goal is for each bed to feed our household through August, with extra for the neighbors.

Packing for the trip to Chicago went smoother than I expected, mostly because I made a list the week before. Last time I flew to a wedding I brought three pairs of dress shoes and wore none of them, so this round I sorted everything by what I would actually use. The formal attire went in one garment bag, and the casual clothes went in a cube organizer so nothing wrinkled. I still forgot a phone charger, which is why I now keep a spare in the bag.

My rule now is a single carry-on and one personal item, which fits under the seat and skips the baggage line. I roll the shirts and fold the jacket on top, and I keep liquids in a quart bag near the front. For documents I photocopy the passport and the ID and stash the copies in a separate pocket, so if the originals go missing I have something to show the airline. The wedding invitation goes in the tote, since the hotel desk asked for it once before.

Next month I am heading to a conference in Denver, and I plan to use the same system with one change. I will pack the business attire in tissue so the collars stay crisp, and I will keep a small steamer in the bag. My coworker Ines swears by compression packing cubes, so I will test a pair this time. Once I get back, I will note what I did not touch and drop it from the list. That list will be the only thing I reuse, because every trip seems to need something different.

I replaced the chain on my old road bike last month, and I learned a few things the hard way. The old chain had stretched past the point where the cassette could hold it, and the ride started skipping under heavy pedaling. I bought a new chain and a chain checker, which is a cheap little tool that measures wear. The reading came back at 0.75, which is past the usual cutoff, so the chain had to go. Getting the old pin out with a breaker tool took longer than the swap itself.

Now the new chain runs quiet on the big ring and the small cog, and I keep it clean with a dry lube after every wet ride. I wipe the chain with a rag, then put a single drop on each roller and let it sit overnight. Grit is the enemy, so I never spray degreaser straight onto the bearings. My riding club holds a monthly luncheon at a diner near the reservoir, and the mechanic there, Walt, always checks my chain before the group heads out. He is the one who told me to measure it earlier.

Next season I plan to swap the chain every three thousand miles and replace the cassette at the same time, since they wear together. I will buy the parts in a pack so the shifting stays crisp, and I will set aside an afternoon before the first group ride. The new chain complies with the spec the manufacturer lists, which matters for the warranty on the drivetrain. This was the cheapest lesson I could have learned, and the bike has never shifted better.

Sunday started badly. Marisol's braise recipe called for six bone-in thighs and I only had four, so I dug through the freezer and found a bag of wings from August. Making alterations to the plan seemed sensible at the time. Four thighs, nine wings, a cup of stock from the ice cube trays, and a pot of white beans that had soaked overnight and were now going soft at the edges. I used the chipped Dutch oven because it holds heat better than anything else I own.

Browning took forever. The skin wouldn't release from the pot until I stopped poking it, which Marisol says is the whole trick and which I keep forgetting. I left the wings for the last batch because they needed the fat to render. The kitchen filled up with that smell, paprika and garlic and something a little scorched on the bottom of the pan, and I stood there with the spatula thinking the whole apartment would smell like this until Tuesday. Fancy bread would have been nice, but I only had the heel of a baguette, so that went into the sauce.

Honest verdict: the beans were the best part. Nobody asked for them, and I almost didn't make them, but the thighs sat on a bed of those beans and soaked up everything the pan gave off. Marisol texted at seven asking how it turned out. I sent a photo of the pot with the lid off and wrote back that I had no idea what I'd done but I'd do it again. She replied with one word, Wings?, and I laughed out loud, alone in the kitchen. I wonder whether she'll ever make the dish without me telling her what to skip.

Every Tuesday I take the old road bike out before work, and this morning the front derailleur is clicking again. I think it's the cable. Ozzie says it's the hanger, and we have been arguing about it over text since last week. The bike is a 1987 steel frame I bought from a guy in Yonkers who apologized the whole time for the paint. I like it more than almost anything I own. The saddle is still too high, or too low, depending on the day, and the handlebars sit at a height my lower back has opinions about.

The ergonomics thing is what I keep coming back to. Ozzie measured everything with a string and a level, and now the saddle sits two centimeters lower and the bars drop a little. My shoulders hate me less. The first ride after the change feels like riding a different bike, which I suppose is the point. The roadway down the county route is narrow with no shoulder for about a mile, and that's where the motorists get impatient. Yesterday a box truck passed so close I could feel the air push my jersey against my back.

I stay loose and stay right. I ride where the tire marks are, because that's where the glass collects least. Ozzie's rule is simple: assume the driver in the blue sedan hasn't seen you. Most days he's wrong, and most days I'm lucky. The gears are fine when the chain is clean and the cassette isn't full of grit, and I spend most of the ride thinking about the clicking, which in the end comes down to a stretched cable I can fix with a five-millimeter hex key and some patience.

Practice starts the same way every day, with the metronome at 60 and my hands feeling like they belong to someone else. Renna wants the left hand to sing under the melody, not wander off, and so far my left hand keeps wandering. The piece is the Nocturne in E-flat, the slow one, and I've been living inside bars nine through sixteen for three weeks. Those bars have a shape I can't quite hear yet. Firstly, I need to stop rushing the turn in bar twelve, where the right hand has to leave the melody alone for a moment and let the chords breathe.

Today something fell into place, mostly by accident. I played the left hand alone, very slowly, counting out loud the way Renna makes me, then put the right hand in on top without thinking about it. The melody came out beautifully for about four measures before I lost it again. That's the fusion she talks about, when two separate jobs become one thing. My pedal still smears the chords, though. I lift too late on the downbeat of bar fourteen, and the room fills with a muddy sound that Renna once described as a wet dog in a closet.

Her note from last week is still taped to the music stand: Sing it, don't play it. I keep forgetting. I play it like an exam, each note checked off before I move on. The good moments happen when I stop listening for mistakes and just let the phrase lean forward. Tomorrow I'll record the first ten bars on my phone, because the recording will tell me the truth faster than my ears do. Then I'll sit with cold tea and listen back, probably wincing, probably hearing one thing I can fix.

The cucumber beetles arrived in the second week of July, all at once, the way they always do. I'd been so proud of the squash. Lorne gave me the seedlings in May, four of them in yogurt cups, and by late June the leaves were the size of dinner plates. Then the beetles found them. They chewed holes along every leaf edge and sat in the blossoms like they owned the place, tiny yellow-green things with black stripes that I kept mistaking for loose bits of leaf.

I tried everything for about ten days. I went out at dawn with a cup of soapy water and knocked them off one at a time. I bought neem oil and read the label twice before mixing it, then spent an hour on my knees with the spray bottle, going over the undersides of the leaves while the neighbor's dog watched me through the fence. The neem helped some. Lorne came over on a Saturday, took one look at the plants, and gave me the stark truth: by August the squash would be finished no matter what, so save what you can and move on.

We pulled the two worst plants that weekend. The other two I kept, covered the hills in row cover, and weighed the edges down with bricks. The next morning I found the bricks scattered and the cover ripped in one corner, which I assume was a raccoon with a grudge. I want to try again next year, earlier, before the beetles wake up. Lorne says to plant three weeks sooner and tuck marigolds between the hills. I wrote that on the back of the seed packet, which is now stained green and smells faintly of the garage.

Last Thursday's class was supposed to be about trimming, and I spent the whole evening on a mug I wanted to be a bowl. Cass showed us how to center the clay, which I did, mostly, and then I pulled the walls up too thin. The mug collapsed on itself twice. The third time I gave up on making it tall and just made it a mug. Whichever bit of clay I touched next seemed to go wrong, so I stopped touching it for a while and watched the other people at their wheels.

Ignacio, who is retired and makes enormous ugly bowls, wedged his clay like he was kneading bread against an enemy. Dagny was throwing vases with a precision I found a little unsettling. My mug finally stood up straight on the fourth try. Cass ran her thumb around the rim and said it was lovely, then she ran a wire under the base and the handle, which I'd stuck on too early, slid right off. It ripped clean from the body. I actually laughed. Clay has no mercy for people who rush.

I'm going back next week to redo the handle, this time scoring both surfaces and using slip the consistency of heavy cream. Cass says the kiln shelves are the real test, since the firing shows everything. The mug is drying on a board under plastic, with a strip of masking tape on it that says handle, round two. I keep looking at it on my kitchen shelf, the lumpy blue thing, and it's already the best thing I've made.

The desk came off a curb near the bus stop with a cardboard sign that said free and a little arrow. I carried it home alone, which in hindsight was not the safest decision I've made this year. Pilar came over with her cordless drill and a pot of coffee and said the veneer on top was lifting near the back left corner and the drawer runners were shot. We spent the first afternoon just looking at it. The oak underneath was gorgeous once the dust came off, and under the dust was a green paint somebody had brushed on in 1974.

Stripping took a long Saturday. I used a citrus gel, scraped it off with a plastic putty knife, and wiped everything down with mineral spirits until the rags stopped coming up brown. The top had a dark ring near the center, probably from a plant pot, so I tested a rouge-colored dye on a scrap of oak before committing. It was too pink. Pilar thought it was too orange. We settled on a warm reddish brown that looked like wet clay after rain, and I brushed it on in thin coats, one hand, no drips.

The drawers were the real fight. The runners had worn into little grooves, so I shimmed the sides with thin strips of cedar and glued them in place. Then I waxed the fixtures and tested each drawer ten times until it slid without a squeak. I still need new brass pulls, because the originals are missing. Pilar says the hardware shop downtown carries a set in the right size. I moved the desk to the back porch to let the finish cure, and the afternoon light caught the grain, and I stood there longer than I needed to.

I am sitting on the back steps with binoculars in my lap and a cup of coffee going cold, which is how every good morning starts now. The house wren is back in the nest box on the fence post. Teodor says the pair has been using that box since April, but I only noticed last week, when the male started singing from the top of the rain gutter. He is loud for something so small. The song runs fast and bubbling, like someone pouring water from a height.

Teodor showed up this morning with a field guide in a plastic sleeve and an old pair of binoculars with a scratch across one lens. He doesn't mind the scratch. He walked me through the difference between the house wren and the Carolina wren, which is harder than the book makes it sound, and I wrote down what I could hear. The Carolina wren is bigger and sharper and sings teakettle, teakettle. The house wren is plainer and looser. The stark truth is my ears are worse than my eyes. Every time I think I've learned one call, another bird starts up in the hedge.

The part that gets me is how much goes on in one small box. The female flies in with grubs and spiders, back and forth, every few minutes, all day. She hardly rests. I counted twelve trips in half an hour. I wonder how she keeps track of where every spider is. There's something about that work that makes the whole yard feel larger, as if I've lived next to a city for years and only now opened the window. I'll keep the notebook on the steps tomorrow. Teodor says to watch for fledglings in June, when they sit on the fence in a row, not quite ready to fly.

Book club was at Wilhelmina's place this time, which meant we sat on her enormous couch and argued about everything except the book. The book was a novel called The Salt Ferry, which I'd started and dropped in March. I finished it on the bus this week. Firstly, the opening hundred pages are slow, and then the last third turns into a storm. Half the group loved the ferry captain. The other half wanted to throw him in the harbor. I was in the second half.

Dolores had seen a stage version where the captain is played by an actor with a limp, and she said the limp made the whole plot make sense. The rest of us thought that was too neat. Whichever side you took, everyone agreed the sister's letter in chapter nine was the best thing in the book. Lars brought a bottle of cheap sparkling cider, and nobody touched the cheese. Wilhelmina kept checking the clock, which I took as a sign she was having fun.

I was the one who wanted the ending to be sadder. I said so, and Wilhelmina asked why, and I didn't have an answer beyond a feeling about the rain on the last page. Then I realized the rain was the best part, because the author never explains it. Next month we read something shorter, a story collection by a woman from Lisbon, and I'm pretty sure I'll finish it by Tuesday. I'll bring the sister's letter printed out, because I want to read it aloud and see who cries.

Next Saturday I'm going to bake my first real loaf from the starter Hollis gave me. Her starter is called Gus, and Gus is going to be fed twice on Friday night so he's bubbling and ready by morning. I'll mix the flour and water at seven, let it rest for an hour, then add the salt and start folding. I'm told the folds matter more than the timing, which sounds like a riddle, but I'll write it down anyway. The loaf will probably come out flat. That's fine. Flat bread is still bread.

After the bake I'll spend the afternoon cleaning my counter, which is the part I actually dread. Hollis says a light spray of water on the oven walls makes the crust crackle, and I'm going to test that with a fancy spray bottle I bought for my plants. The bottle will be useless for plants and perfect for bread. I'll stand at the counter with my back straight, because Hollis insisted on ergonomics: the bench should sit at elbow height, and I'll stop hunching over the dough like a gargoyle. I'll set a timer for twenty minutes and then another for forty.

Afterward I'll wait to cut the first slice until it has cooled enough to stop steaming into a gummy mess, which will be hard. I plan to write down the temperature of the kitchen, the hydration percentage, and whether the crumb looks the way the photos in the book do. If it doesn't, I'll adjust one thing at a time: less water, a longer rest, a hotter oven. Hollis will come over for the taste test and tell me the truth about the flavor. I'll wait for her verdict before I decide anything.

The morning walk started on the shoulder of the county roadway, the one with no sidewalk and a painted line that gets fainter every year. Motorists come fast around the bend by the feed store, so I wear the orange vest Delphine bought me and keep my ears open. I passed a man walking a basset hound who said good morning like he meant it. Then I came home and had coffee, which is one of the only ordinary things I still do the same way every day. I was thinking about the scarf the whole time.

The scarf is a seed stitch in a dark green wool that was on sale. I cast on in March, ripped it out twice, and cast on again. The first attempt was too tight. The second was wide enough to wrap a small car. This third one feels right, though I'm down to the last few rows and my count keeps drifting. Delphine's birthday is Thursday, and I told her it would be finished, which is a claim I'm now testing. My hands ache a little from holding the needles so tight. I should loosen my grip, which my knitting group keeps saying in one form or another.

Tonight I'll finish the last inch and weave in the ends. Then I'll wash it gently in cool water with a drop of soap and lay it flat on a towel to dry. Tomorrow I'll give it to Delphine wrapped in brown paper. She will probably notice the one lumpy section near the end, where I got distracted talking to a neighbor on the phone. I'm going to tell her that's the part that's mine. Honestly, I like that it's imperfect. Everyone's scarf is a little bit about the hour it took.

Last spring I took the 7:12 train out of Hempstead every morning for eleven weeks, and I still think about that commute more than I should. The train was never on time, the seats smelled like wet umbrellas, and the guy across from me always ate a hard boiled egg at 7:40 sharp. I used the ride to read the same long article on bridge design four times, because I kept losing my place whenever the doors opened. My friend Dana kept telling me to just drive, but the parking garage cost more than my lunch budget and I hated the idea of sitting in traffic on the parkway.

The real problem was that nobody around me was doing anything useful with their time. People stared at their phones or closed their eyes and waited. So I decided to treat the train like a small office. I had to activate offline mode on my laptop before we reached the tunnel, because the signal always died under the river. Some mornings I wrote a rough outline for a grant proposal that eventually got funded. It was not glamorous. My coffee spilled twice, and one draft got smeared with the sticky cinnamon bun I bought at the station kiosk.

The article I kept rereading was reprinted from a magazine nobody reads anymore. The author argued that a commute is only wasted if you let it be wasted. I thought that was a smug line when I first read it. By week nine I believed it a little. I still think driving is faster for most people, and I am not going to pretend the trains fixed my life. But they gave me eleven weeks of uninterrupted thinking, and that is worth more than the forty minutes I lost each day.

My son Owen gets a math worksheet every night, and every night the same fight starts at the kitchen table. I think homework should be short. The sheet he brings home has thirty problems on long division, all printed in the same layout, and he counts them out loud before he even picks up his pencil. Owen tells me he is done before he has started. The teacher says the repetition builds fluency, which sounds fine in theory, but the repetition is what annoys him, not the math. A kid who is bored on page one is not learning anything on page three.

I sat with him last Tuesday and timed the work. The first ten problems take him eleven minutes, mostly because he holds the pencil like a fork and his number strokes come out so messy that he cannot read his own carries. The middle ten take nine minutes. The last ten take twenty, because by then he is crying quietly and erasing through the paper. Holding the sheet up to the window, I can see the answers are right. The math is not the problem. The length is the problem, and the handwriting is the problem, and nobody is grading either one.

So here is what I plan to send the school board this week. Cap nightly math at twenty minutes. Send home five problems that matter instead of thirty that repeat. Let kids type long answers when their handwriting gets in the way. I know a few teachers will push back, and some of them have good reasons. Still, a worksheet a child dreads teaches him to dread the subject, and that is the one lesson I would rather he never learns from our kitchen table.

People who grew up in cities keep asking me what a small town actually gives you, and I always answer with the fountain in our square. Carrow Falls has one cast iron fountain, painted green every spring by whoever has a free Saturday, and it is the center of almost everything. Kids wade in it in July. Old men argue about the weather at its edge. The fountain has no real purpose except to make people stop and look at each other, and I think that is the whole point of a town this size.

The word local gets thrown around so much that it has lost its meaning, so let me define it. Local is the person who sells you a sleeve of crackers at the feed store and remembers that your dog died. Local is the diner where the waitress knows your order before you sit down. Semantics matter here: a town of two thousand people does not have a mall, but it has a hundred small arrangements that work because everyone knows the names. Nobody writes these arrangements down. They just hold together.

I know the counterargument. Small towns can be suffocating, and everybody knows your business, including the business you would rather keep private. My cousin left at eighteen and never looked back, and I do not blame her. But I have lived in two cities and I still feel more known in a place where the fountain is the main attraction. Some nights I walk to the square, sit on the edge, and count how many people I recognize. The number keeps going up.

Last Thanksgiving my sister Nora put her phone face down next to her plate, and by dessert it had buzzed eleven times. Nobody said anything for the first course. Then my dad asked a question about the gravy, and the whole table reached for their phones at once. I remember thinking that dinner used to be a place where you talked to whoever sat across from you. That year it felt more like a waiting room with mashed potatoes.

I started a rule the next month. Phones went into a wooden basket by the front door, and whoever broke the rule had to do the dishes alone. My husband thought it was silly. My kids thought it was cruel. Still, the first dinner without screens was strange, and conversation came back in strands. Randomly, my dad started humming a song from the sixties, and my youngest told a long story about a field trip. Nora corrected my grammatical slip about who and whom, and we argued about it for ten minutes. Before we knew it we had talked for an hour about nothing in particular.

I know the objections. Some families cannot afford to spend a whole evening unreachable, and I get that. Doctors are on call, and nurses are on call. But most of us are not on call at dinner. We are just scared of the quiet. The basket is still by the door, and when someone forgets to leave their phone in it, my dad reminds them with a look that could curdle milk. That look has been worth more to our family than any app I have ever downloaded.

I am learning Portuguese, and my problem is not vocabulary. I can memorize five hundred words in a weekend. My problem is that the grammar and the words live in separate boxes in my head, and every time I try to use the subjunctive I have to reach across the room to find it. Tight coupling is the phrase my software friend uses. In language learning, it means you should practice verbs inside sentences you actually want to say, not as isolated drills on a flashcard.

So I changed my routine. Every lesson now ends with a short summary I write in my own words, one sentence per idea. If I cannot summarize the subjunctive in a sentence, I have not learned it yet. My conversation partner, Lucia, lives in Porto and corrects me every Tuesday over video. She laughs when I mix up ser and estar, and I laugh when she tells me my accent sounds like a lost tourist. The flashcards are still useful, but they are the warm up now, not the workout.

I think most people quit because they treat the language like a list of parts. Verb tables, noun genders, a pile of rules that never connect to a conversation. Summarize what you did today in the new language, even if it is three clumsy sentences. Describe your breakfast. Describe the bus. The words will stick better when they are holding something real. I still forget half of what I learn, but the half that stays is attached to people, and that is the only kind of memory that has ever helped me talk.

When I was twelve, the Wexley branch library had a basement room full of microfilm readers, and I spent most of my summer down there reading old newspapers because nobody else wanted to. The librarian, Mrs. Abernathy, let me stay until closing as long as I put every reel back in its box. I loved the clatter of the machine and the way the old headlines flickered across the glass. I still think about that room whenever somebody says libraries are obsolete.

The library also ran a book sale every October, and that was where I learned to love reprinted paperbacks from the fifties. Some of them had covers so lurid they annoyed my mother, which only made me want them more. I bought a stack of six for a quarter each and read them under the reading lamp by the fountain in the courtyard, which was a dry bronze thing nobody ever turned on. Those books taught me more about sentence rhythm than any teacher I had.

People argue that libraries are just buildings with books in them, and that the internet made them unnecessary. I disagree, and my reasoning is pretty simple. A library is the only place where a twelve year old can walk in with no money, no membership card, and no reason, and walk out with an armful of strange things. Nobody asks what you are looking for. They just point you toward the basement. That kind of door is hard to build in a search bar.

For three years I worked from a card table in the corner of my bedroom, and I was sure I would hate working from home. I was wrong about the commute and right about nearly everything else. My desk now sits in the spare room, which I have decided to call the office, mostly so I can close the door on my laptop at six. Somehow my stack of printed invoices keeps growing anyway.

The hardest part is the meetings. Every Thursday at ten our team holds a status call that runs forty minutes, and I spend most of it with my camera off, eating a cracker and muting myself every time my cat jumps onto the keyboard. Randomly, someone will ask a question I have clearly not heard, and I have to pretend I was following along. Holding a cup of tea while nodding into a microphone is a skill I did not expect to learn at thirty two.

Here is my honest take. Remote work is great for people who already know how to finish things without a boss standing nearby. It is rough for anyone who needs the building to tell them where the day starts and stops. I think companies will keep pushing people back into offices, and some of that will be fair. But I will keep the door closed at six and the cracker tin on the shelf. Those two habits have done more for my sanity than any productivity app I ever tried.

Next season the Harbor City Gulls will make the playoffs, and I am willing to bet my season tickets on it. The bullpen is deeper than it has been in a decade. Our left side of the infield will be the best in the league, and the young catcher will finally learn to block the ball in the dirt without flinching. People tell me I am being too optimistic. Those people have not been to a game at the stadium since the new seats went in.

Here is the plan. Opening day, I will sit in section 118 with my brother Kenji, and we will activate the wave at least twice before the seventh inning. We will eat the same overpriced hot dogs, and I will almost certainly get ketchup smeared across my good jacket. Kenji keeps a spreadsheet of every pitcher's walk rate, and he will read me strands of numbers all afternoon. I will nod along, even when I do not understand the slope of the curve.

The skeptics will say that baseball is too slow for a generation that scrolls through everything. They may be right about the scrolling. But the summer nights will still belong to the people in the cheap seats, shouting at umpires about balls they could never hit. We will win more games than the experts predict, and the city will finally stop joking about us. I am already picking out the parade route.

My sourdough starter is named Gerald, and he is the most demanding houseplant I have ever owned. Every morning I feed him equal weights of flour and water, and every evening I check whether he has doubled. People assume baking bread is about recipes. It is really about patience and timing. The recipe is just a rough map, and the starter decides where you end up.

The semantics of bread are the part nobody warns you about. A loaf can be underproofed and still look perfect from the outside, while the crumb inside is a gummy mess. You learn to read the dough by touch. You press it gently and watch the dimples spring back. You score the top with a single clean stroke of a razor blade, and if your hand shakes, the bread tears open in the oven. Every loaf teaches me one small thing about restraint.

Store bought bread is fine for sandwiches, and I will not pretend otherwise. But the bread I bake on Sunday has a crust that crackles when it cools and a sour, almost nutty flavor that no bag can match. I bring a loaf to my neighbor Walt every week, and he tells me the same joke about how bread is just flour that got ambitious. He is right. Gerald is ambitious, and so am I.

When we moved onto Linden Street in 2019, the parking situation looked fine on the map. Then the new apartment building opened across the road, and suddenly every curb was taken by nine a.m. I used to park in front of my own house without thinking about it. Now I circle the block like a shark, and I have started to resent the man who parks his truck across two driveways every Sunday.

The problem is tightly tied to the zoning rules. The city approved the building with almost no spaces, which made sense on paper for people who take the bus. In practice, the residents own cars and visit their parents, and their visitors park on our street. I wrote the council a letter that was reprinted in the neighborhood newsletter, and it annoyed one of the building managers so much that he called me personally. We had a cordial conversation, which is the best kind of argument.

I do not think the answer is angry letters. I think the answer is building more parking into the new projects and charging a fair price for the spaces we do build. I also think the people on Linden Street should talk to each other before they call the tow company. Last month Mrs. Okafor and I swapped snow shoveling for parking spots, and the whole block got a little friendlier. Next year I will be the one knocking on doors.
